summary: Introduces an optional Bandwidth Availability TLV in RSVP-TE signaling, for setting up GMPLS LSPs with Ethernet traffic parameters where links such as radio have variable bandwidth. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Some links, like radio ones, slow down in bad weather. This lets a connection ask for bandwidth along with how often it is available.

questions: what is the bandwidth availability tlv
what is link availability in rsvp-te
how does rsvp-te handle variable bandwidth links
subtitle: A new RSVP-TE field that lets an LSP ask for bandwidth together with how reliably that bandwidth must be available.

tldr.problem: Some links, such as microwave or copper, change their bandwidth with weather or interference. A plain bandwidth request does not say how reliably the bandwidth must be there, so it is treated as needing the highest availability and may be refused unnecessarily.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an optional Bandwidth Availability TLV, type 4, carried in the Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC object. Each one gives an availability value that pairs with an Ethernet Bandwidth Profile TLV through a shared Index.
tldr.outcome: Nodes can check each bandwidth request against the remaining bandwidth at the matching availability level, and reserve it or return an error. It is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Error on shortfall
facts.value: Admission Control Error / Requested Bandwidth Unavailable

today: RFC 8625 is a Proposed Standard, published in August 2019. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its routing-side companion is RFC 8330.

sections.title: Links with Variable Bandwidth
sections.content:
RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) and its GMPLS extensions (RFC 3473) signal the bandwidth request used to set up a Label Switched Path (LSP). Some technologies can change their maximum physical bandwidth through a set of known discrete values. Network planners describe such links using availability, the proportion of operating time that the requested bandwidth is ensured.

Different services need different availability. The RFC gives voice as needing 99.999%, while non-real-time services may be fine with 99.99% or 99.9%. So a request may need several <availability, bandwidth> pairs.

Without an availability value, the bandwidth will likely be reserved as the highest availability. In the RFC's example, a link has 100 Mbps at 99.999% and 200 Mbps at 99.99%. A video application asks for 120 Mbps with no availability stated, which is treated as 99.999%, and the LSP cannot be set up even though the video application would be happy with 99.99%. Stating availability in signaling fixes this. The approach applies to any link with variable discrete bandwidth, such as microwave or DSL.
sections.plainLanguage: If you do not say how sure you need to be, the network assumes you need the very safest option and may say no when a lesser guarantee would have worked fine.

sections.title: How the Pieces Fit
sections.content:
To set up an LSP, a node usually learns link information from routing messages such as OSPF TE LSAs, computes a route, and then signals it with PATH and RESV messages. For links with variable discrete bandwidth, the LSP gets a <bandwidth, availability> requirement list at setup, which can come from service planning.

A node with such a link should advertise a list in its OSPF TE LSAs that maps nominal link bandwidth to availability level. That routing side is covered by RFC 8330. This RFC covers the signaling side.

When a node starts PATH signaling, the PATH message carries the requirement list as a bandwidth request. Intermediate nodes allocate resources for each availability requirement from the remaining bandwidth at that availability. An error may be returned if any pair cannot be satisfied.
sections.plainLanguage: The map tells everyone how much room a road has at each level of guarantee, and the booking request asks for room at a specific level.

sections.title: The Bandwidth Availability TLV
sections.content:
The Bandwidth Availability TLV is a new TLV of the Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC object defined in RFC 6003. The object MAY include more than one. Because the Ethernet FLOWSPEC object has the same format, the TLV can also be carried there. It is 12 bytes long.

  • Type (2 octets): 4.
  • Length (2 octets): 0x0C, the length of the whole TLV including Type and Length.
  • Index (1 octet): ties this TLV to an Ethernet Bandwidth Profile TLV with the same Index value. When several bandwidth requirements have different availabilities, multiple TLVs MUST be carried. If all requirements share one availability, one TLV SHOULD be carried and Index is 0.
  • Reserved (3 octets): SHOULD be zero when sent and MUST be ignored when received.
  • Availability (4 octets): a 32-bit IEEE 754 floating-point number, which MUST be less than 1 and is usually 0.99, 0.999, 0.9999 or 0.99999.

The floating-point format aligns with RFC 8330. It starts to lose precision above 0.999999, but the RFC says 0.99999 (about 5 minutes of outage in a year) is normally the highest value in a telecom network, so this is acceptable. When the Bandwidth Availability TLV is included, the Ethernet Bandwidth Profile TLV MUST also be included.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a small form with a few boxes. One box says which bandwidth request it belongs to, and another holds a number like 0.9999 that says how sure the guarantee must be.

sections.title: The Signaling Process
sections.content:
The source node sends a PATH message that may carry several Ethernet Bandwidth Profile TLVs and Bandwidth Availability TLVs. Each profile TLV corresponds to an availability parameter in its matching availability TLV. Intermediate and destination nodes compare each requested bandwidth with the remaining local link bandwidth at the corresponding availability level.

  • If every pair can be satisfied, the node SHOULD reserve bandwidth from each remaining sub-bandwidth portion. Optionally, higher-availability bandwidth can be given to a lower-availability request when the lower portion cannot satisfy it.
  • If at least one pair cannot be satisfied, the node SHOULD generate a PathErr message with error code "Admission Control Error" and error value "Requested Bandwidth Unavailable" (see RFC 2205).

When two LSPs request bandwidth with the same availability, contention MUST be resolved by comparing node IDs, and the LSP with the higher node ID gets the reservation. This follows Section 4.2 of RFC 3471.

A node that does not support the TLV should send a PathErr with error code "Unknown Attributes TLV" (RFC 5420), though the LSP could still be set up if there is enough bandwidth, with the availability of the reservation unknown. A message MUST be ignored and MUST NOT be propagated if it mixes zero and non-zero indexes, if a non-zero index has no matching Ethernet Bandwidth Profile TLV, or, for extra profile TLVs that match no availability TLV, those extra TLVs are ignored and not propagated.
sections.plainLanguage: Each stop along the way checks whether it has room at the asked-for guarantee level. If yes, it holds the room. If not, it sends back a message saying it cannot.

sections.title: A Microwave Link Example
sections.content:
Appendix A uses a microwave link with adaptive modulation. In heavy rain the link lowers its modulation level, which needs a lower signal-to-noise ratio but also gives less bandwidth. The link has three discrete levels: 100 Mbps (for example QPSK), 200 Mbps (16QAM) and 400 Mbps (256QAM). On a sunny day, 400 Mbps is available.

In the example, light rain drops the link from 400 to 200 Mbps. That rain level occurs 52 minutes in a year, so the bandwidth lost has 99.99% availability. Heavy rain drops it from 200 to 100 Mbps, occurs 26 minutes in a year, and the lost bandwidth has 99.995% availability. The final 100 Mbps is lost only in extreme weather, for 5 minutes in a year, so it has 99.999% availability.

The result is a set of buckets that sums to the 400 Mbps maximum: 200 Mbps at 99.99%, 100 Mbps at 99.995% and 100 Mbps at 99.999%.
sections.plainLanguage: When it rains, the road shrinks. The last small strip almost never disappears, so it is the most dependable part. The extra lanes that vanish when it rains are less dependable.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security section is short. It points out that RFC 3945 says authentication in GMPLS systems may use the mechanisms of the component protocols. RFC 5920 gives an overview of GMPLS control plane security, including protection of RSVP-TE using general RSVP security tools, limiting the impact of attacks, and authentication of RSVP messages. A GMPLS network is also often considered a closed network where outsiders cannot insert, modify or inspect packets.

For IANA, the "Ethernet Sender TSpec TLVs/Ethernet Flowspec TLVs" subregistry of the GMPLS Signaling Parameters registry was updated with type 4, Bandwidth Availability, referencing RFC 8625.
sections.plainLanguage: The message uses the same safety tools as the rest of the system, and the new form was given its own official number, 4.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the whole TLV in bytes, including Type and Length.

fields.name: Index
fields.desc: Matches an Ethernet Bandwidth Profile TLV with the same Index; 0 if one availability covers all.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero when sent, ignored when received.

fields.name: Availability
fields.desc: 32-bit IEEE 754 floating-point value, less than 1, such as 0.9999.
